name: Lele
confidence_why: one confirmed first-hand source; 1 other work read was silent
catalog_citation: Boettger, Juliane. 2015. Topics in the grammar of Lele: a language of Manus Island, Papua New Guinea. PhD thesis, James Cook University. researchonline.jcu.edu.au/41204/
catalog_locator: Ch. 2, §2.3 'Phonological Word', pp. 43-44 (thesis pagination); also §2.1 vowel allophony p. ~38-39 and Ch. 1 conclusion-preview on future research
catalog_quote: A phonological word in Lele can be defined using the following criteria: 1. The phonological word cannot be interrupted 2. There is one main accent assigned to each phonological word 3. Aspiration of plosives is optional, but occurs particularly on word boundaries, cf. (2.1.1.2) 4. Glottal stops only occur at the beginning of words ... Word stress is difficult to predict and must be considered idiosyncratic to the word. However, future research is necessary.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim at the stated locator in the extracted text we hold of the JCU thesis PDF. The deciding source is the sole and most recent full description of the language (2015, 415 pp, fieldwork-based), so nothing better is known to exist; the classification lexical ('unpredictable/idiosyncratic to the word', one main accent per phonological word) faithfully renders the author's statement, and her own stress-marked transcriptions show variable stress position on disyllables. The record is 'adequate' rather than 'well-sourced' only because the source's stress treatment is a single hedged sentence flagged for future research, not an analysed stress system; not determinable would be a defensible alternative label but no evidence points to a different positive coding.
